citations.quote: The general form of a recursive WITH query is always a non-recursive term , then UNION (or UNION ALL ), then a recursive term , where only the recursive term can contain a reference to the query's own output.

Evaluate the non-recursive term. For UNION (but not UNION ALL ), discard duplicate rows. Include all remaining rows in the result of the recursive query, and also place them in a temporary working table .
So long as the working table is not empty, repeat these steps:
When working with recursive queries it is important to be sure that the recursive part of the query will eventually return no tuples, or else the query will loop indefinitely.

questions.notes: Base/recursive split, repeated evaluation against the working table, empty-result termination and UNION dedupe versus UNION ALL are all correct.

citations.quote: When using LIMIT , it is a good idea to use an ORDER BY clause that constrains the result rows into a unique order. Otherwise you will get an unpredictable subset of the query's rows
Thus, using different LIMIT / OFFSET values to select different subsets of a query result will give inconsistent results unless you enforce a predictable result ordering with ORDER BY .
It is even possible for repeated executions of the same LIMIT query to return different subsets of the rows of a table, if there is not an ORDER BY to enforce selection of a deterministic subset.

questions.notes: Correct: a non-unique ORDER BY leaves tied rows unordered between executions, so OFFSET paging can duplicate or skip rows; a unique tiebreaker fixes it. Keyset pagination is a correct additional remedy.

citations.quote: If neither is specified, the default behavior is NULLS LAST when ASC is specified or implied, and NULLS FIRST when DESC is specified (thus, the default is to act as though nulls are larger than non-nulls).

citations.quote: By default, the CREATE INDEX command creates B-tree indexes, which fit the most common situations.
B-trees can handle equality and range queries on data that can be sorted into some ordering.
B-tree indexes can also be used to retrieve data in sorted order.
Hash indexes store a 32-bit hash code derived from the value of the indexed column. Hence, such indexes can only handle simple equality comparisons.

questions.notes: Correct contrast: B-tree is the default and handles equality, range and ordering; hash handles equality only.

citations.quote: PostgreSQL supports building indexes without locking out writes. This method is invoked by specifying the CONCURRENTLY option of CREATE INDEX .
Thus this method requires more total work than a standard index build and takes significantly longer to complete.
If a problem arises while scanning the table, such as a deadlock or a uniqueness violation in a unique index, the CREATE INDEX command will fail but leave behind an “ invalid ” index.
Another difference is that a regular CREATE INDEX command can be performed within a transaction block, but CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot.

questions.notes: Correct: CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes, costs more work/time, leaves an invalid index on failure, and cannot run in a transaction block.

corrections.from: An indexed varchar column code is compared as WHERE code = 42 while the application sends an integer parameter. Why might the index not be used, and what is the clean fix?
corrections.to: An indexed varchar column code is compared as WHERE code = 42 while the application sends an integer parameter. What happens, and what is the clean fix?
corrections.reason: The statement fails with an operator-resolution error; it is not a silent planner fallback.

corrections.from: The comparison involves a type conversion that may not match the index operator class; compare with the same type or index the expression.
corrections.to: There is no varchar = integer operator, so the statement fails with an operator-resolution error; send '42' as text or use an explicit cast, and index the cast expression if the cast is intended.
corrections.reason: Verified against PostgreSQL 17.11; the original understated the failure.

corrections.from: An index is defined for a column type and its operators. Comparing a varchar column with an integer forces a conversion, and the planner may not be able to use the plain varchar index operator class. The clean fix is to compare values of the same type, for example by passing a string parameter, or to create an expression index that matches the expression if a cast is intentional. Nullability and work_mem are unrelated.
corrections.to: PostgreSQL resolves operators by argument types. There is no character varying = integer operator, so WHERE code = 42 raises 'operator does not exist: character varying = integer'. Passing the value as text keeps the existing varchar = varchar operator and the plain index usable. If a cast on the column is intended, such as code::integer = 42, the plain varchar index no longer matches and an expression index on the cast is required. Nullability and work_mem are unrelated.
corrections.reason: Corrects the failure mode and the fix while keeping the same concept and difficulty.
Cite the section that defines exact-match and implicit-conversion operator resolution.
